q: Is induction cooking lower carbon than LPG in a factory canteen or hotel kitchen in India?
title: Induction vs LPG in a canteen kitchen
short: Not on India's grid average today. Per unit of heat reaching the pan, induction at 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh emits roughly one and a half to two times the CO2 of an LPG burner. Induction becomes the lower carbon choice when the electricity comes from rooftop solar or another renewable supply.
audience: Hotels, institutional kitchens and factories with canteens

sections.h: Compare per MJ of useful heat
ul: LPG: 2.98 kg CO2 per kg / (47.3 MJ per kg x stove efficiency). At 55 percent efficiency that is 0.115 kg CO2 per MJ in the pan; at 40 percent, 0.158.
Induction: 0.710 / 3.6 MJ per kWh / induction efficiency. At 85 percent that is 0.232 kg CO2 per MJ.
p: Stove efficiencies here are labelled estimates. Large commercial burners and open flames sit at the low end; well-maintained burners with the right pan size do better.

sections.h: The grid factor at which induction wins
p: Induction matches a 55 percent efficient LPG burner when electricity carries about 0.35 kg CO2 per kWh, and a 40 percent burner at about 0.48. The CEA average is 0.710, so induction loses on location-based accounting. Power from your own rooftop solar, or renewable power backed by certificates under market-based Scope 2, can bring it below those figures.

sections.h: How the switch shows in your inventory
ul: LPG burnt in your kitchen is Scope 1.
Electricity for induction is Scope 2, reported location-based, and market-based if you hold renewable instruments.
Do not report a cut in Scope 1 as a saving without adding the new Scope 2.

sections.h: Reasons to switch other than CO2
p: Kitchens move to induction for indoor air quality, cooler working conditions, cylinder safety and supply risk. Those can be good reasons. Just do not claim a carbon saving unless the electricity is cleaner than about 0.35 to 0.48 kg CO2 per kWh.

example.title: Worked example: a hotel kitchen using 1,000 kg of LPG a month
lines: Heat in the pan at 55 percent: 1,000 x 47.3 x 0.55 = 26,015 MJ
Same heat by induction at 85 percent: 26,015 / 0.85 / 3.6 = 8,502 kWh x 0.710 = 6,036 kg CO2
If the LPG burners were only 40 percent efficient: 18,920 MJ, so 6,183 kWh x 0.710 = 4,390 kg CO2
Either way induction on grid power emits more; on rooftop solar the Scope 2 figure falls toward zero
example.note: Efficiencies are labelled estimates; measure your own with a water-boiling test. LPG 2.98 kg CO2 per kg and NCV 47.3 MJ per kg are IPCC 2006 defaults.

senseible: Senseible reads LPG invoices at 2.98 kg CO2 per kg and electricity bills at 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh, so the canteen's Scope 1 and Scope 2 before and after a switch come from your own documents.
